description: Mater Amabilis Year 1 living books curriculum for grades K-1. Emphasis on oral narration, nature observation, and wonder-filled discovery through short, rich lessons.

books.title: Aesop's Fables
books.author: Aesop
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: Oral narration focus. One fable per sitting. Ask the child: 'What did you learn from that story?' Let them discover the moral themselves.

books.title: Just So Stories
books.author: Rudyard Kipling
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: Read aloud for rhythm and delight. Kipling's language is a feast — don't rush. Narration: 'Tell me how the elephant got its trunk.'

books.title: Winnie-the-Pooh
books.author: A. A. Milne
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: Mater Amabilis prizes literature that illuminates character. Focus on Pooh's friendship with Piglet. One chapter per session.

books.title: Fifty Famous Stories Retold
books.author: James Baldwin
books.subject: history
books.notes: Heroic tales from history retold simply. Perfect for narration — 'Tell me the story of William Tell in your own words.' Builds historical imagination.

books.title: Among the Meadow People
books.author: Clara Dillingham Pierson
books.subject: nature_study
books.notes: Gentle nature stories told from an insect's perspective. Pair with outdoor observation. Ask: 'Have you seen a grasshopper like this?'

books.title: Secrets of the Woods
books.author: William J. Long
books.subject: nature_study
books.notes: First-hand naturalist accounts. Long observed animals directly and writes with the excitement of discovery. Ideal for nature journal follow-up.

books.title: Understood Betsy
books.author: Dorothy Canfield Fisher
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: A timid city girl discovers competence and freedom on a Vermont farm. Rich in Mater Amabilis values — independence, real work, nature. Best for late Year 1 or early Year 2.

books.title: A Child's History of the World
books.author: V. M. Hillyer
books.subject: history
books.notes: A narrative sweep of world history from creation to modern times, written for children. Read two to three pages per sitting. Pair with timeline entries.

books.title: Trial and Triumph: Stories from Church History
books.author: Richard Hannula
books.subject: saints
books.notes: Inspiring true stories of Christians throughout history. One story per week. Ask: 'What made this person brave?' and 'How could you show that virtue today?'

books.title: The Complete Tales of Beatrix Potter
books.author: Beatrix Potter
books.subject: living_books
books.notes: Potter was a naturalist as well as an artist. Note the botanical and animal accuracy alongside the story. Read one tale per session.

books.title: Handbook of Nature Study
books.author: Anna Botsford Comstock
books.subject: nature_study
books.notes: Parent reference for guiding nature study. Use specific sections when the child encounters a bird, insect, or plant. Don't read cover to cover — consult as needed.

books.title: Pilgrim's Progress (abridged for children)
books.author: John Bunyan
books.subject: saints
books.notes: Use a children's adaptation. The allegory is rich for narration — 'What do you think the Slough of Despond means for us today?' Connect to the child's own faith journey.

subject_plans.art_music: Composer: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart — joyful, clear melodic lines, an ideal first composer for young ears. Listen to short, contrasting pieces (a symphony movement, a piano sonata, an aria) across the term, always the same composer, so the child begins to recognize his 'voice.' Artist: Vincent van Gogh — bold color and texture children respond to immediately (Sunflowers, The Starry Night, Wheatfield with Cypresses). Look at one picture per sitting, in silence first, then narrate what is seen before any facts are given. Poet: Christina Rossetti — short, musical poems written with children in mind (Sing-Song). Read aloud for rhythm and delight; memorization of a favorite stanza is welcome, analysis is not.
subject_plans.greek: Year 1 scope (grades K-1) — the alphabet, by ear and eye. Two or three letters a session: their names, their sounds, their shapes, traced in the air or on paper. Alpha and Beta first, because the word ALPHABET is those two letters stuck together and a child delights in owning that. Alpha and Omega together as the year's anchor — the first letter and the last, and Christ calling himself both. Alongside the letters, the sounds of pistis, elpis, and agape, always with the English beside them. No reading of Greek words, no grammar, no translation. Getting through half the alphabet in a year with real delight is a better year than getting through all of it grimly. Everything in this year is the shared inheritance of all Christian traditions — the Greek New Testament, the theological virtues, and the ordinary vocabulary of the faith — so a Protestant, Catholic, or Orthodox family can teach it in full. Introduce nothing specific to one tradition here (devotion to the saints or to Mary, the sacraments, prayers for the dead, icons, a particular church's authority or structure), and take no position on which Greek manuscript tradition is correct: every text supplied reads the same in both. Send any doctrinal question that divides Christian traditions to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister. All Greek quoted must come from the verbatim block supplied in the session — never recited from memory, never composed — and always shown with its transliteration and English.
subject_plans.language_arts: Grade K/1: oral narration only — never require written composition at this age. Copywork is a single short sentence or a few words, hand-picked from that day's living book, focused on letter formation and the pleasure of beautiful handwriting rather than length. Phonemic awareness and reading practice happen alongside, not through this tutoring session. 'Tell it back to me in your own words' is the whole of narration at this stage.
subject_plans.latin: Year 1 scope (grades K-1) — Latin by ear alone. The child hears a word, says it back, and learns what it means in one short sentence; nothing is written, parsed, or translated. Across the year: Fides, Spes, Caritas as sounds and simple meanings (trust, looking forward, love that gives itself away), plus Deus, Amen, Lux, and Pax. The two halves of Christ's summary of the law — 'Diliges Dominum Deum tuum' and 'Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum' — are met as two short phrases to say aloud together, never as a translation exercise. Two or three words in a session is a full lesson, and saying last week's word again is better than adding a new one. Delight is the whole measure at this age: a child who shouts LUX for the joy of the sound is doing exactly what is asked. Everything in this year is the shared inheritance of all Christian traditions — the Vulgate, the theological virtues, and the ordinary vocabulary of the faith — so a family of any Christian tradition can teach it in full. Introduce nothing specific to one tradition here (devotion to the saints or to Mary, the sacraments, prayers for the dead, a particular church's authority or structure); a family that wants that has Saints & Catechism as its own subject. Send any doctrinal question that divides Christian traditions to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister. All Latin quoted must come from the verbatim block supplied in the session — never recited from memory, never composed.
subject_plans.mathematics: Grade K/1 scope (Common Core domains K.CC, K.OA, K.G, K.MD): counting and cardinality to 20 and beyond; one-to-one correspondence; comparing quantities (more/fewer/equal); simple addition and subtraction within 10 using real objects, never abstract algorithms first; recognizing and naming 2D/3D shapes; measurable attributes (longer/shorter, heavier/lighter). Mater Amabilis approach: manipulatives (buttons, blocks, fingers, nature-study specimens) and real-life counting (setting the table, counting steps) before any worksheet or written number sentence.
subject_plans.morning_time: Opens with a short Scripture passage read aloud (a Gospel story or Psalm verse is ideal at this age), a simple hymn or folk song sung together, and a few lines of that term's poet (Christina Rossetti). Keep each element brief — a few minutes each — and warm rather than instructional.
subject_plans.science: Year 1 scope — the science of noticing: living and non-living; what animals need; parts of a plant; the five senses; day and night; hot and cold; things that float and sink; weather from the window. Charlotte Mason approach: science at this age IS nature study plus honest wondering. Ask what the child observed, never what they remember being told.
subject_plans.scripture: Year 1 scope — Bible narrative, told as story: creation; Noah; Abraham's call; Joseph and his brothers; the baby Moses; David and Goliath; the birth of Jesus; Jesus blessing the children; the Good Shepherd. One short memory verse per term, chosen by the family. Charlotte Mason approach: read or tell the passage once, unhurried, then ask the child to narrate it back in their own words before any discussion. The narration IS the comprehension check — no quiz. Keep to what the text plainly says; questions of doctrine belong to the family's own pastor or priest. Canon and translation are the family's own: follow whatever Bible they are reading and never assert that one tradition's canon, chapter ordering, or translation is the correct one. Teach the narrative and the moral law the text plainly states; leave denomination-specific doctrine — sacramental theology, church governance, a particular catechism's structure — to the family's own pastor, priest, or minister.
